message.content:
The answer is no.
Under the usual definition, a finite expectation requires absolute integrability.
Thus if both expectations are finite, each variable is integrable.
An integrable sum is also integrable.
The sum of integrable discrete variables is integrable.
Therefore the expectation of the sum exists.
It is finite.
It equals the sum of the expectations.
No counterexample exists in that setting.
The apparent ambiguity comes from conditioning on signs.
Positive and negative parts are separately finite.
Those parts control the behavior of the sum.
Conditional convergence is not the standard meaning here.
Reordering terms is not allowed for expectations.
Expectation uses the absolute integral, not an ordered series.
So the answer is negative.
This conclusion holds for discrete variables.
It also holds for general measurable variables.
Finite marginal expectations imply finite joint integrability of the sum.
The sum cannot be undefined if the parts are finite.
It cannot be infinite either.
The construction is impossible.
The decisive reason is that, under the standard definition of expectation, the expected value of the sum is controlled by the finite positive and negative parts for any such pair of random variables beneath the standard integrability condition.
